trajectory_summary: This is a short, efficient rebooking call: the rep re-engages a known lead whose prior appointment fell through, gets a scheduling constraint, briefly mishears the customer's preferred day, corrects within seconds, and locks a specific day and time. The call is thin on substance — no re-qualification, no probe into why the first meeting didn't happen, no bill or interest reinforcement — but it accomplishes its narrow goal cleanly and quickly.
outcome_dispute: If v1 tagged this as anything other than booked, that is miscalled: a specific date (the 29th) and time (6:00) are both confirmed verbally by the customer at 01:27-01:30. This should be recorded as booked, phone channel, datetime captured.

observed_outcome.reasoning: Customer explicitly confirms a specific day (Wednesday the 29th) and time (6:00) verbally, and the rep restates it back at 01:33 — this meets the bar for a booked appointment with a specific date and time, not merely tentative.

bill_anchor_audit.reasoning: No bill amount or usage figure is discussed anywhere in this transcript — the call is purely a rescheduling/rebooking exchange, likely because bill data was already captured on a prior touch.

interest_reason_audit.reasoning: The rep never asks what interested the customer in solar, and the customer never volunteers a reason — consistent with this being a second-touch rebook where that qualification presumably happened on a prior call not captured in this transcript.

script_coverage.quote: This is Brandon with Ion Solar.
Just reaching back out about that design for your home.
Yeah. I could do Wednesday at six?

primary_coaching_focus.quote: Alright. That's the twenty ninth at 06:00. Okay. Good deal. Okay. Great.
primary_coaching_focus.why: The rep locks a date and time efficiently but skips every confirmation mechanic (hour block, no-driving instruction, verbal handshake, text-follow-up promise) that the schema ties directly to show-rate. This is the single most fixable, highest-leverage gap on an otherwise clean, short call.

key_moments.quote: Hi. If you record your name and reason for calling, I'll see if this person is available.
key_moments.stewart_read: This call opens through what sounds like a screening assistant or gatekeeper system rather than the customer picking up directly, which explains why the rep's actual intro to the customer at 00:27 lands abruptly with no separate legitimacy-building beat — the rep had already stated his name/reason to the gatekeeper at 00:07.

key_moments.quote: Yeah. Hello, Brian. This is Brandon with Ion Solar. How are you doing?
key_moments.stewart_read: The rep states his name and company but gives no anchor for why he's calling beyond the immediately-following design reference — there's no state/referral-source framing at all. Given this is a rebook of an existing lead, full legitimacy-building is less critical than on a cold call, but some anchor beyond name+company is still schema practice.

key_moments.quote: We didn't get a chance to meet with you last week, so I was calling to see if you'd be available.
key_moments.stewart_read: The rep acknowledges a missed prior appointment but never asks why it was missed (schedule conflict? cold feet? competitor interference?). On a rebook call this is the one piece of free competitive/behavioral intelligence available, and it's skipped entirely in favor of jumping straight to new scheduling.

key_moments.quote: That's the only way I could do it. Thursday. Do you have anything late or not really?
key_moments.stewart_read: Customer states a hard after-5:30 constraint. The rep never anchors call length or duration expectations (no 'it's a 30-minute call' statement per protocols.time_constraint) despite the customer's evening-time pressure signaling a busy schedule — a missed chance to set a firm time expectation that reduces no-show risk.
